forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of $2.01 remains 17% above the Street consensus of $1.72, reflecting what I believe is systematic underestimation of mechanical EPS drivers that are largely independent of top-line performance. Wall Street appears anchored on depressed sentiment following the Wine & Spirits divestiture and CEO transition, creating a sentiment-driven discount rather than a fundamentally-justified one. The key insight is that three quantifiable factors—accelerated share buybacks at depressed prices (170.8M shares vs 174.6M in Q3), declining interest expense (~$82M vs $87M in Q3), and SG&A normalization to ~$355M from Q3's bloated $491M—provide mechanical EPS uplift that the Street is underweighting.

The revenue story is straightforward: Q4 is seasonally the weakest quarter for STZ, and I expect $2.17B consistent with prior year patterns. The beer segment remains stable with flat to -1% volume trends validated by Molson Coors' Q4 transcript showing healthy North American category dynamics. Gross margins should hold at 52-53% on the beer-focused mix, with operating leverage from SG&A normalization driving the EPS beat. The Q3 SG&A spike to $491M included non-recurring items that won't repeat; Q4 should normalize to ~$355M including roughly $10M of CEO transition costs.

Key risks to my above-consensus call include: (1) deeper-than-expected consumer pullback in premium beer, (2) higher CEO transition or restructuring costs, and (3) tax rate volatility from annual true-up adjustments. However, absent material negative surprises on these fronts, the mechanical share count reduction and interest expense decline should drive reported EPS well above the depressed consensus. I would revisit my estimate if we see evidence of accelerating beer volume declines or if management signals elevated one-time costs in any pre-earnings commentary.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 remains $0.04 (7.3%) below the Street consensus of $0.55, as I continue to believe analysts are systematically underweighting the mechanical tax rate normalization headwind. Q4 2025's reported EPS of $0.52 was significantly aided by an anomalously low 2.6% effective tax rate ($109M on $4.26B pretax income), driven by discrete tax benefits that management explicitly stated will not recur. With the company guiding to a 21% effective tax rate for 2026, this creates approximately $750-850M in incremental quarterly tax expense versus Q4, translating to roughly $0.10-0.11 EPS headwind that must be offset by operational improvements.

The operational picture is solid but insufficient to offset this tax headwind. I expect Mobility service revenue growth of ~3% YoY, supported by stable postpaid phone net adds in the 400-450K range and continued fiber momentum of ~250K net adds. However, Q1 faces seasonal equipment revenue decline of ~16% from Q4's holiday peak, reducing total revenue from $33.5B to approximately $30.5B. The AT&T Guarantee expansion announced this week (adding Internet Air and free backup) is retention-positive but not a material near-term revenue driver. The CAD-denominated notes filing suggests ongoing debt management rather than any fundamental change.

What would change my view: If AT&T realizes meaningful discrete tax benefits in Q1 (similar to Q4), my estimate would be too conservative. I'm also watching the Barclays conference for any CFO comments that might suggest tax rate flexibility below 21%. Additionally, if postpaid phone net adds significantly exceed 500K or fiber net adds top 300K, the service revenue beat could partially offset my tax concerns. My conviction is medium - the tax math is mechanical and clear, but there's inherent uncertainty in discrete items.

forecasts.thesis:
I am forecasting Q1 2026 EPS of $0.56, slightly ahead of the $0.55 consensus. My variant view is anchored in a granular analysis of the 'Profitability Mix Shift' specific to Q1. The Street often straight-lines margins, but Q1 historically features a ~30-35% sequential drop in low-margin equipment revenue while high-margin Service revenue (Mobility/Fiber) remains sticky. This mechanical mix shift expands blended margins more than the consensus model appreciates.

Key data points supporting this include the confirmed Q4 2025 equipment seasonality trend and the sustained growth in Fiber ARPU. While interest expense ($1.83B/qtr) is a confirmed headwind preventing a larger beat, the underlying operational efficiency from the cost transformation program creates enough buffer to deliver a 1-cent beat. I also note that the consensus likely underestimates the OpEx leverage gained from recent headcount rationalization.

Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging that if post-paid phone churn surprises to the upside (above 0.85%), or if promotional activity in the sector spiked violently in Feb/Mar (unseen in current data), my margin expansion thesis would crumble. Additionally, if the recent CAD debt filing signals a higher-than-expected cost of refinancing, the interest expense line could erase the operational beat.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY2026 forecast of -$0.04 EPS on $318M revenue represents a modest bullish revision from my prior $315M estimate, driven by stronger-than-expected traction from Good Supply's high-THC product lineup. The cannabis segment is showing pricing stability contrary to bearish narratives, with the premium vape category (91-97% THC) commanding meaningful price points that support improved mix. I'm raising my cannabis revenue estimate to $86M from $84M based on this momentum.

The critical swing factor remains SG&A normalization. Q2's $102M included what appears to be one-time professional fees and restructuring costs - my thesis assumes Q3 returns to a more sustainable ~$95M run-rate. If correct, this $7M reduction flows directly to EBIT and gets us to near-breakeven normalized operations. The BrewDog acquisition (announced March 2) is strategically sound but won't contribute until Q4 at earliest per the 8-K terms.

I diverge from the historical average consensus of -$0.22 EPS because that figure is skewed by massive non-cash impairments in prior quarters (Q4 2025 had $1.75B loss, Q3 2025 had $1.14B). On a normalized operating basis, Tilray has stabilized significantly. The peer data from Nextleaf showing profitability validates the sector can achieve breakeven with disciplined cost management. Key risk: if Q2's elevated SG&A was structural rather than one-time, my EPS could miss by $0.04-0.06 to the downside.

forecasts.thesis: My differentiated view: The Street's consensus EPS of -$0.22 is dramatically too optimistic, ignoring substantial near-term acquisition integration costs and accelerating cash burn. The BrewDog acquisition (closed in Q3) adds approximately $25M revenue but brings $20M+ in one-time integration costs, inventory step-up expenses, and acquisition-related depreciation that compress gross margins to ~24.3% (vs historical ~26-30%). While beverage growth accelerates (+28.5% YoY) and new cannabis products add ~$5M revenue, these are offset by elevated SG&A from acquisition integration (+$15M QoQ) and persistent cash burn (~$40M in Q3 from acquisition outflow). The company continues to rely on dilutive equity issuance to fund operations, with shares outstanding increasing to ~113M. The key data points driving my variant view: (1) Historical cash burn of ~$15M quarterly plus $45M acquisition outflow, (2) SG&A increasing sequentially by ~$15M with acquisitions, (3) BrewDog beer business operates at lower margins than Tilray's historical beverage segment. I would change my mind if: (1) Management reveals BrewDog integration costs are below $10M, (2) Cannabis pricing stabilizes and shows +10% sequential growth, (3) Operating cash flow turns positive excluding acquisition costs.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.72 remains 2.9% above the consensus estimate of $0.70, maintained from my prior forecast as no material new information has emerged since March 5th. United Community Banks continues to execute well on its core strategy of NIM expansion through disciplined deposit pricing and loan repricing benefits. Management's Q4 earnings call emphasized 11% year-over-year revenue growth, and I expect this momentum to continue with NII reaching approximately $242M (+1.7% QoQ) as the bank benefits from fixed-rate loan repricing while deposit costs stabilize around 2.1%.

The key differentiator in my above-consensus view is the expectation for operating expense normalization. Q4's elevated $168.7M operating expense figure included what appears to be one-time items, and I project a return to the ~$156M run-rate seen in prior quarters. This expense leverage combined with continued NII growth should drive operating income improvement. The recent regional bank sector selloff following February inflation data creates near-term sentiment headwinds but does not alter the fundamental trajectory for UCB, which maintains strong credit metrics with stable NPAs and low substandard loans.

What would change my view: If operating expenses fail to normalize (staying above $165M), that would reduce my EPS estimate by $0.05-0.07. Additionally, any unexpected credit deterioration in the CRE portfolio or accelerated deposit competition pressuring NIM would be concerning. However, with institutional ownership at 82.29% and analysts maintaining a Buy rating with a $37.33 price target, the fundamental investment case remains intact despite sector headwinds.

My variant view versus consensus is minimal and centers on execution quality rather than topline growth. The Street appears to be appropriately skeptical following Q1's miss, reflected in the 'Reduce' average rating and $181 price target (vs current ~$235). What would change my view: if Cintas talks conclude (either way), removing uncertainty around buybacks and management focus, or if we see evidence of accelerating customer churn or pricing pressure from competitors like Vestis. The binary M&A outcome remains the dominant swing factor that could render operational forecasts largely moot.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.88 represents a modest $0.03 increase from my prior $1.85 estimate, but remains approximately 5% below Wall Street consensus of $1.97. The primary driver of my below-consensus stance is that the Street appears to be over-extrapolating from Valero's strong H2 2025 performance (Q3 at $3.66, Q4 at $3.82) without adequately discounting Q1's structural seasonal headwinds. Q1 is historically Valero's weakest quarter due to peak turnaround season reducing throughput and utilization rates, fading heating demand, and the gasoline blend season not yet beginning. The Q1 2025 result of -$1.90 EPS illustrates extreme downside potential, though conditions this year are materially better.

The incremental upside to my estimate comes from three factors: (1) mid-quarter crack spread data showing resilience at $15-17/bbl versus feared sub-$15 levels, supported by geopolitical tensions; (2) peer read-throughs from Phillips 66 trading at 52-week highs suggesting sector fundamentals are holding better than feared; and (3) continued share count reduction to ~300M shares from 303M, providing ~1% EPS accretion. However, the renewable diesel segment remains a persistent drag with the 10-K filing (Feb 25, 2026) confirming no near-term improvement catalyst for the ~$150M quarterly losses.

I would increase my estimate toward consensus if: (1) crack spreads sustain above $17/bbl through March; (2) turnaround schedules compress with no unplanned outages; or (3) renewable diesel margins show unexpected improvement. Conversely, I would reduce my estimate if crack spreads fall below $14/bbl or if refinery utilization drops below 85% due to operational issues. The key differentiator from consensus is my more conservative gross margin assumption of 7.2% versus what appears to be Street expectations closer to 8.5-9%, reflecting my view that seasonal dynamics matter more than recent momentum.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.18 sits 2.5% below Wall Street consensus of $1.21, reflecting persistent concerns about January network outage fallout and Frontier integration friction that I believe the Street is underweighting. The key variant perception is that CEO Schulman's explicit acknowledgment of 'failing to meet customer expectations' signals deeper churn issues than consensus models, while the $250M+ sponsorship review announced today confirms cost pressures are real. However, I'm raising my estimate from $1.17 to $1.18 based on improved institutional sentiment (JT Stratford +300%, Crossmark +3.4% position increases) and the cost-cutting signals suggesting management is actively addressing the margin compression.

The fundamental setup shows mixed signals: Q4 2025 delivered six-year high postpaid net adds, but Q4 EPS of $0.55 dramatically underperformed prior quarters ($1.17-$1.19 range) due to elevated operating expenses and one-time items. I'm modeling Q1 revenue of $33.7B (+0.7% YoY) with Frontier contributing ~$1.9B conservatively versus Street estimates above $2B, as integration friction typically runs higher in first full quarters. Interest expense of ~$1.78B remains a $150M YoY headwind from Q4 debt issuances, and I expect incremental churn costs of $50-75M from the January outage that won't fully appear until mid-quarter data becomes visible.

What would change my view: If early March churn data shows normalization (which we can't yet observe) or if management signals stronger-than-expected Frontier contribution at an investor event, I would revise upward toward consensus. The 34.8% surge in short interest to 148.3M shares validates the bearish positioning, but the stable analyst consensus at 'Hold' with $49.80 target suggests limited downside from current $44 levels. The 6.5% dividend yield provides valuation floor, making this a moderate-confidence call rather than high-conviction short.

The consensus forecast of $1.21 implies an acceleration in growth that contradicts the typical Q1 seasonal lull and the current frictional costs on the balance sheet. I see the business fundamentally healthy but technically weighed down in Q1.

I would revisit this thesis if VZ announces an earlier-than-expected close to the Frontier deal (removing the negative carry) or if subscriber data indicates the outage had zero net churn effect. However, the math on the debt service vs. interest income is an unavoidable arithmetic headwind for this specific quarter.

With projected ending cash of approximately $5M and quarterly cash burn of $8-10M, Waldencast faces an immediate existential funding requirement. The Pomerantz securities investigation adds legal cost burden and management distraction at the worst possible time. While Q4 underlying operations should show modest sequential improvement from Q2's disaster quarter (driven by typical holiday seasonality for Milk Makeup), any operational analysis is highly speculative given the information vacuum.

I would increase my estimate if: (1) the company finally reports earnings without a going concern qualification or restatement, (2) they announce a financing package with reasonable terms, or (3) Milk Makeup holiday sell-through significantly exceeded expectations. Conversely, I would reduce my estimate further if the delay extends past mid-March, if a going concern qualification is issued, or if additional goodwill impairment is required. My conviction remains low given the extreme uncertainty - essentially this is a placeholder estimate pending actual disclosure.

The Q1 FY26 SG&A spike to $63.5M—representing a $10-12M elevation above the historical $51-54M quarterly range—was attributed to distribution transition costs that management indicated would persist through FY26. While I expect modest sequential improvement to ~$61M as some one-time costs abate, the structural cost elevation from the new distribution model should prevent a rapid return to the ~$58M level that consensus appears to be assuming.

My revenue estimate of $160M reflects typical Q2 seasonal strength (historically WDFC's strongest quarter), with Americas expected to benefit from both normal seasonality and modest TikTok-driven demand visibility among younger consumers. However, the key differentiator in my forecast versus consensus is on the cost side: I'm projecting gross margin of 55.2% as the Q1 inventory build of $84M flows through COGS, and SG&A of $61M reflecting only partial cost absorption from the distribution transition. This yields operating income of ~$27.2M and net income of ~$20.5M, translating to diluted EPS of $1.36.

Key risks to my thesis include: (1) faster-than-expected SG&A normalization if management front-loaded transition costs in Q1, which would push me toward consensus; (2) stronger-than-expected Americas demand from viral marketing, which could drive upside to my $160M revenue estimate; and (3) FX movements that could swing either direction given WDFC's significant international exposure. The pattern of institutional exits (APG -61%, Vanguard earlier reduction) suggests sophisticated investors share concerns about near-term margin pressure, reinforcing my below-consensus stance.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 remains 3.9% above the Street consensus of $1.52, reflecting my view that the market is still anchored to Q4 2025's weather-disrupted results and underweighting the structural recovery underway. Three quantifiable factors support this above-consensus view: (1) Brent crude has averaged ~$78/bbl in Q1 2026 versus ~$73/bbl in Q4 2025, providing approximately $1.5B in incremental upstream revenue given XOM's ~3.8Mboe/d production and high exposure to international pricing; (2) Guyana operations are now at full Payara capacity (220kbpd with sub-$35/bbl breakevens), contributing premium margin barrels that the Street chronically undervalues; and (3) Gulf Coast operations have normalized after the January freeze disruptions that drove the 7.8% Q4 miss.

The Street appears to be making two key errors. First, analysts are extrapolating Q4's -7.8% miss into Q1 estimates despite the one-time nature of the freeze impact. The 10-K filed February 18 confirmed this was operational disruption, not structural deterioration. Second, consensus models appear to lag crude price realizations - Brent's Q1 average is ~$5 higher than Q4, yet the $1.52 consensus implies minimal upstream recovery. My revenue build shows $82.8B (vs Q4's $80.0B), driven by upstream price uplift and downstream normalization post-turnaround season.

What would change my view: If refinery turnarounds extend beyond planned schedules (cutting ~200kbpd throughput), I would revise down by $0.03-0.05. If chemical margins fail to stabilize as destocking completes, that's another $0.02 downside risk. However, the Hormuz disruption creating routing flexibility for XOM's Gulf Coast barrels (600k shipment to Australia noted in recent news) provides incremental upside optionality not in my base case.

My forecast of $1.68 EPS stands 10.5% above the consensus of $1.52, driven by a structural disagreement on how XOM captures 'volatility bookends.' Wall Street is seemingly extrapolating the Q4 earnings miss ($1.53) into a linear trend, ignoring that Q1 2026 featured two distinct profit accelerators: the January North American freeze which benefits XOM's premier gas portfolio, and the March geopolitical crude spike which XOM's Global Trading division is uniquely positioned to arbitrage. While consensus models likely reflect average quarterly prices, they often miss the 'convexity' of earnings during spot price spikes.

Institutional selling reported today (Pitcairn/Edgar Lomax) is interpreted here as backward-looking portfolio rebalancing rather than a signal of fundamental deterioration. Operational data remains robust, particularly the continued volume ramp in Guyana (Payara/Prosperity) which enhances the corporate mix shift toward higher-margin barrels. The Street underestimates the operating leverage in the Upstream segment when localized gas realizations spike, even if the headline Henry Hub price for the full quarter looks average.

What would change my mind: Evidence that the Q4 earnings miss was driven by sticky structural cost inflation (OpEx/Capex) rather than one-time maintenance or timing effects. If refining cracks compress significantly faster than the geopolitical risk premium adds to crude realizations, the integrated model's hedge effect could turn into a drag, pulling EPS closer to the $1.55 range. However, current data supports the volatility upside case.

forecasts.thesis:
I am maintaining my ¥43.50 Q4 2026 EPS estimate, which represents a 6.2% discount to the Street consensus of ¥46.39. My variant view centers on continued skepticism about the pace of operating margin recovery. While Q4 should see meaningful seasonal improvement from Q3's severely depressed 7.3% operating margin, I project only 10.7% recovery versus the 11.0%+ embedded in consensus. The key constraint remains the persistent inventory overhang at ¥216.5B (as of Q3), which improved only marginally despite management's efforts to accelerate destocking. Until I see evidence of meaningful inventory normalization toward the ¥200B level, margin recovery will remain constrained.

The revenue picture is more constructive, with my ¥148.5B estimate representing healthy sequential growth and modest YoY improvement. Motion Control should benefit from Japan/US stabilization, though China weakness (approximately 30% of segment revenue) continues to be a drag. Robotics benefits from semi equipment stabilization noted in peer commentary, though auto sector softness persists. System Engineering remains the steady performer with infrastructure backlog providing visibility. The Hyster-Yale Q4 2025 results released this week show mixed industrial equipment demand signals, which neither confirms nor contradicts my baseline assumptions for YASKAWA's end markets.

What would change my view: If I saw (1) inventory declining below ¥205B indicating genuine destocking progress, (2) China orders inflecting positively based on channel checks or peer commentary, or (3) management raising guidance in a meaningful way that suggests better visibility. Conversely, risks to my estimate include China demand deteriorating further, inventory destocking stalling, or auto sector capex cuts accelerating. Given the data uncertainty and margin recovery thesis still unproven, I maintain medium conviction on this forecast.
